Read a parquet file straight onto the GPU

Source: R/io.R
read_parquet_gpu.Rd

read_parquet_gpu() decodes a parquet file on the GPU with libcudf, so the file's compressed bytes are what cross the PCIe bus (DECIMAL columns are converted through the host, see Types). Like tbl_gpu() it respects the execution mode: a lazy table (the default) holds a scan that reads the file when the plan runs, an eager one reads it now. The column names and types come from the file footer at call time without reading any data. write_parquet_gpu() writes a GPU table with libcudf's writer.

Usage

read_parquet_gpu(path, columns = NULL, lazy = NULL)

write_parquet_gpu(.data, path, compression = "snappy", row_group_size = NULL)

Arguments

path

For read_parquet_gpu(), one path or a vector of paths, read in order. The files must have the same column names, in the same order, with the same types. libcudf also requires their footers to describe the columns identically, including parquet's type annotations, so files from different writers can be refused even when the columns agree (DuckDB annotates INT32 columns and arrow does not): that is a cuplyr_error_parquet_schema_mismatch when the read runs. For write_parquet_gpu(), one path (an existing file is overwritten).

columns

Optional character vector (not empty): read only these columns, in this order. A column that is not read is never decoded, so a file with a column cuplyr cannot hold is readable as long as that column is left out.

lazy

TRUE, FALSE, or NULL for the session default, as in tbl_gpu().

.data

A tbl_gpu. A lazy plan is run first (it stays lazy: the table you passed is not changed), groups are not written.

compression

"snappy" (the default), "zstd", "lz4" or "none".

row_group_size

Rows per row group, or NULL for libcudf's default (one million).

Value

read_parquet_gpu(): a tbl_gpu. write_parquet_gpu(): .data, invisibly.

Details

Types

BOOLEAN, INT32, DOUBLE, STRING, DATE and microsecond timestamps read as themselves. INT64 reads as integer64 (exact, no downcast; with the bit64 package). FLOAT reads as double, INT8/INT16/UINT8/UINT16 as integer, UINT32 as double, UINT64 as integer64 (an error naming the column if a value is past INT64_MAX), DECIMAL as double (the nearest one, with a cuplyr_warning_collect_precision warning if more than 15 digits are needed; the conversion runs on the host, so a DECIMAL column makes a round trip over the PCIe bus), second, millisecond and nanosecond timestamps as POSIXct (nanoseconds finer than a microsecond are rounded, with that warning). LIST, STRUCT and TIME columns are an error of class cuplyr_error_parquet_unsupported_type naming the column and the file when a plan reads the column. columns = always keeps it out of the read. A later select() usually does too, but a verb that has to run the plan before the select() (an integer sum() in mutate(), for example) reads every column, so use columns = if you get this error.

An INT32 or INT64 value equal to -2147483648 or -9223372036854775808 is read as missing: R's NA_integer_ and bit64's NA are those values, so R (and arrow's read_parquet()) cannot hold them as numbers, and a filter or a sum on the GPU has to agree with collect().

Factors

A factor written by write_parquet_gpu() comes back as the same factor (levels, unused levels and ordered), because the levels are kept in the file footer. A factor with NA as a level (addNA()) is the exception: a file cannot tell that level from a missing value, so write_parquet_gpu() warns (class cuplyr_warning_parquet_factor_na_level, naming the column) and the column reads back as strings, with the missing value as NA. A factor written by arrow::write_parquet() reads as a string column: arrow keeps the levels in the parquet dictionary pages, which libcudf does not expose. If you need the factor, convert it afterwards, e.g. mutate(f = factor(f, levels = ...)) on the collected data.

Time zones

A POSIXct column written by write_parquet_gpu() or by arrow keeps its time zone. A timestamp with no zone information in the file (no ARROW:schema entry, e.g. written by another tool) is read as UTC instants with tzone = "UTC". A timestamp arrow wrote without a zone (isAdjustedToUTC = false) is read as UTC instants and has no tzone attribute, as in arrow.

If the file changes

A lazy table remembers the columns and types the file had when read_parquet_gpu() was called. The plan reads the file again every time it runs. If the columns or their types differ then, the read stops with an error of class cuplyr_error_parquet_schema_changed naming the file and the difference. If only the data changed (same columns, other rows), the new data is read: a lazy scan sees the file as it is when the plan runs, not as it was when the table was made. The row count nrow() of a bare scan comes from the footer at the time you ask. Reading one lazy table twice reads the file twice.

Errors

All errors have class cuplyr_error_parquet and a more specific one, and name the file: cuplyr_error_parquet_not_found, _invalid (not a parquet file, corrupt footer), _unsupported_type, _schema_changed, _schema_mismatch (files that differ), _unknown_column and _columns (columns = names no column or is empty), _write and _compression. Several files are read by one libcudf call that doesn't say which file a problem is in, so those messages say "one of the parquet files". Running out of GPU memory is cuplyr_error_gpu_oom, with the file in the message.

Writing

write_parquet_gpu() writes to a temporary file beside path and renames it into place, so a failed write leaves an existing file as it was. It needs write permission on the directory, not only on an existing file.

Pushdown

When a lazy plan over a scan runs through the optimizer (compute(), collect()), the scan reads only the columns the plan uses, and the conditions of a filter() directly on the scan that libcudf can decide exactly are given to the reader, which skips row groups from the file's statistics and drops the other rows while decoding. explain() shows the columns and the filter of the scan. A condition is pushed only when it is a comparison of a column with a literal that converts to the column's file type without change (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=) on an integer, integer64, Date or POSIXct column, or !is.na() of an integer or integer64 column; the &s of a condition are split. Comparisons on double and string columns are not pushed: libcudf 25.12 can skip a row group wrongly from a double column's NaN statistics or a string column's deprecated min/max statistics (signed byte order), which would lose rows. They are applied after the read, so a filter on doubles or strings gives the same rows but skips no row groups. A factor written by arrow::write_parquet() reads as a string (see above), so it is not pushed either. Everything else (|, !, is.na(), %in%, arithmetic, functions, a double literal against an integer64 column, a column that was converted on reading such as a factor, a filter on a grouped table, with .by, or on a rowwise table, a filter that comes after a mutate() that changes its column, or after a slice(), distinct() or summarise()) is applied after the read, as without pushdown, and a filter with anything left to apply is applied whole. The answer is the same either way. options(cuplyr.parquet_pushdown = FALSE) turns both pushdowns off.

A file whose footer statistics are malformed (for example a fixed-width statistic of the wrong length; an invalid file that no common writer produces) can crash the R session when a filter is pushed into the scan. For files you don't trust, options(cuplyr.parquet_pushdown = FALSE) avoids it.

Previews

print() and glimpse() of a table that is a bare scan (or only select()s and rename()s of one) read just the first rows of the file, which libcudf decodes as whole row groups: when the row group that holds them has more than 65,536 rows or 128 MB of column data, nothing is read and the schema is printed instead (write files with smaller row groups, row_group_size =, to get a preview). Any other plan over a file prints its schema and is not run.

File access

libcudf's file layer (kvikio) is put in its compatibility mode, reading through the page cache, unless the environment variable KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE is set before the first parquet file operation. Set it to AUTO or OFF to let kvikio use GPUDirect Storage where it is installed; that loads libcufile, which writes a cufile.log into the working directory.

When it loads, cuplyr sets the environment variable LIBCUDF_USE_DEBUG_STREAM_POOL, a libcudf debug switch that makes libcudf use its default CUDA stream instead of forking new ones. After parquet reads or writes, forked streams slowed later arrange(), filter() and summarise() calls in the session by a few percent; with the switch on, reads and writes of the files measured, up to 1e8 rows, were no slower. A value you set before loading is left alone, but libcudf only tests whether the variable exists, so any value, 0 included, turns the switch on. To turn it off, call Sys.unsetenv("LIBCUDF_USE_DEBUG_STREAM_POOL") after loading cuplyr and before the first read_parquet_gpu() or write_parquet_gpu() call in the session. A lazy read_parquet_gpu() counts too: it runs libcudf's reader when it is called. libcudf creates its stream pool once, so unsetting the variable later has no effect.

See also

tbl_gpu(), collect.tbl_gpu()

Examples

library(dplyr)
if (has_gpu()) {
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
  write_parquet_gpu(tbl_gpu(mtcars), path)
  read_parquet_gpu(path) |>
    filter(mpg > 25) |>
    collect()
  unlink(path)
}
